exhibit TN enrichment after acidification; no linear fitting was applied to these data points.
For both our new study and compiled datasets of global marine sediment samples, acid
treatments using 1–6 M HCl have generally shown limited effects on nitrogen measurements.
Previous studies reported no significant differences in mean TN content (for 1 M, 2 M, and 6
M HCl) or δ¹⁵N values (for 1 M and 2 M treatments) between acid-treated and untreated marine
sediment samples, with the mean offset for 6 M HCl remaining below 0.2‰ (Kennedy et al.,
2005). Compiled data from marine sediments, suspended particulate organic matter, and marine
biological materials further support this, showing that most δ15N differ by <0.5‰ following
acid treatment, with an average shift of only 0.16‰ (Schlacher and Connolly, 2014). Moreover,
comparing δ15N and TN within the same core, analyzed using identical procedures, helps
minimize potential biases from analytical artifacts and ensures that relative patterns in TN and
δ15N remain reliable (Meyers et al., 2019). Finally, whether the acid effect is considered
‘significant’ depends on the specific research question (Schlacher and Connolly, 2014), as the
shifts in both δ15N and TN induced by acid treatment are often minor relative to the large-scale
patterns and variability of nitrogen signals in global marine sediments (Figs. 1, 3, and 4).
Despite the number of paired analyses conducted, we acknowledge that our dataset does
not allow us to fully resolve the combined effects of carbonate characteristics (i.e., terrigenous
versus marine biogenic origins), the isotopic composition of associated organic and inorganic
nitrogen, and the susceptibility of different N-containing compounds to acid treatment (e.g.,
Kennedy et al., 2005; Walthert et al., 2010; Brodie et al., 2011; Schlacher and Connolly, 2014).
These processes likely interact in complex ways, influencing both the magnitude and direction
of shifts in TN content and δ¹⁵N values. Future work incorporating compound-specific isotope
analyses, metal–nitrogen associations, and controlled experiments of different marine settings
with well-characterized carbonate mineral (terrigenous & marine) endmembers will be essential
to disentangle these mechanisms and better constrain the extent to which carbonate-related
dilution, isotopic fractionation, and nitrogen volatility contribute to the observed variability.
Overall, these results reinforce the broader conclusion that, although acidification can alter
sample chemistry through carbonate removal or alteration of nitrogen-containing compounds,
the magnitude of isotopic shifts is generally minor and unlikely to compromise the reliability
of bulk TN and δ¹⁵N measurements in 15N-enriched marine sediments. After considering your
valuable comments, we have added a detailed description of the procedures (Lines 625–658),
associated figures (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13), and the original data (%C, %TN, δ¹³C, and
δ¹⁵N) from paired analyses of acid-treated and untreated marine and terrestrial samples to the
Supporting Information (Supplementary Tables 8 and 9). In the main text, we have also clarified
the constraints of our study based on combined datasets from both acidified and untreated
analyses (Lines 520–530). We believe these additions ensure full transparency, allowing
researchers to directly assess the effects of acidification on elemental and isotopic compositions
across different sample types, and provide further insight into the mechanisms by which acid
treatment influences nitrogen in diverse marine settings.
2. On a similar topic, I am extremely skeptical of the insights based on the refractory
digestion in the later portions of the paper and, chiefly, in Figure 6. All organic nitrogen
compounds contain carbon and the impacts of this digestion on nitrogen composition
are, as far as I can tell, unconstrained. The original application of this refractory
digestion was to establish the radiocarbon age of the residual pool and it seems like
careful experimentation would be needed to confidently apply and interpret its effects
on total nitrogen and nitrogen stable isotopes. I also suspect its impacts on carbon
stable isotopes are also poorly constrained.
Response: Many thanks for this valuable comment. As you noted, the chemical oxidation
(refractory digestion) was originally developed to isolate residual carbon pools for radiocarbon
dating, and that its direct application to nitrogen and stable isotope systematics is less well
constrained. In this study, we employed the method in an operational sense—consistent with
its broad use in soils, riverine materials, and rocks—to differentiate refractory OC from more
labile marine C pools and thus to quantify the nitrogen associated with refractory organic matter.
To address your concern, we first conducted eleven replicate blank analyses under
identical protocols to those applied to refractory sediment samples. Total OC and nitrogen
concentrations in aqueous solution were quantified using an elemental analyzer (TOC-L,
SHIMADZU, Japan). The mean blank values (±1σ) were 0.408 ± 0.04 ppm for OC and 0.004
± 0.003 ppm for nitrogen, the latter close to analytical uncertainty (~0.004 ppm). These
correspond to only 0.023 ± 0.01% and 0.001 ± 0.0004% of the mean OC and TN contents in
measured refractory marine sediment samples (N = 75; Fig. 5c and d), respectively—orders of
magnitude smaller than sample values and well below the analytical uncertainties of particulate
OC and TN. This demonstrates that blank-derived OC and TN have no significant influence on
δ13C and δ15N measurements.
Secondly, it is important to note that the chemical oxidation approach is designed to
differentiate 13C- and 15N-depleted refractory terrestrial OC from the relatively 13C- and 15N-
enriched labile fraction of marine origin. Consistent with this principle, our results show
significant (P < 0.05) decreases in both δ15N and δ13C values for the refractory OC in marine
org
sediments (Fig. 5d). In other words, when the target of oxidation is inert terrestrial material, the
treatment is not expected to alter the isotopic composition of OC or nitrogen sediment samples,
keeping it within the terrestrial end-member range.
To further verify this assumption, we conducted comparative paired chemical oxidation
experiments on rock samples (N = 24) from the Yangtze River basin (Supplementary Table 10),
dominated by graphitic refractory OC that is largely resistant to oxidation (Galy et al., 2008).
We found that the chemically oxidized samples exhibit comparable average values relative to
unoxidized counterparts: OC (1.2% vs. 1.5%), TN (0.121% vs. 0.129%), δ13C (–27.1‰ vs. –
org
27.0‰), and δ15N (2.5‰ vs. 2.3‰). As shown in the following figure (now Supplementary Fig.
14), although oxidation may remove a minor labile fraction, the OC and TN content, as well as
δ13C and δ15N values of these refractory rock samples, remained statistically unchanged (P >
org
0.05, Wilcoxon test) and consistently fall within the terrestrial range (–25‰ to –30‰; δ15N <
+4‰; Peterson and Howard, 1987; Fogel and Cifuentes, 1993; Goñi et al., 2008). These results
support the robustness of the oxidation approach in distinguishing refractory from labile pools
while minimizing isotopic artifacts. They also provide confidence that the isotopic shifts
observed in marine sediment samples are not analytical artifacts of the procedure, but instead
reflect genuine differences in composition of refractory versus labile organic matter.
Although this approach is applied here for the first time to disentangle the association
between N and refractory OC, we argue that chemical oxidation provides a novel approach for
partitioning the nitrogen–refractory OC coupling and their isotopic composition. Our results
show that the N is significantly (P < 0.001) correlated with refractory OC in marine sediments
from the East China Sea (Fig. 5a), likely also in other river-influenced continental margins,
which together account for majority of sedimentary total N (~68%; Supplementary Fig. 11).
This perspective opens new opportunities for tracing how terrestrial inputs and burial processes
regulate the balance between labile and refractory nitrogen pools, and for assessing their imprint
on long-term carbon–nitrogen burial in marine sediments.

materials, concluding that in two-thirds of comparisons, δ¹⁵N differed by less than 0.5‰ (mean
δ¹⁵N difference for all datasets <0.2‰). Additionally, Walthert et al. (2010) showed that
although some individual samples fell slightly outside the defined precision bands, the overall
differences in TN content were small for untreated (0.5–10.1 g kg⁻¹) versus acid-fumigated
samples (0.5–10.4 g kg⁻¹ for 8h and 0.5–10.7 g kg⁻¹ for 32h, under same 37% HCl). Although
inconsistencies exist between acidified and non-acidified treatments of TN and δ¹⁵N in global
marine sediments, relying solely on non-treated datasets is insufficient to capture their full
global distribution. While some biases may be introduced by different treatment methods (e.g.,
Schlacher & Connolly, 2014; Walthert et al., 2010; Brodie et al., 2011; Kennedy et al., 2005),
the resulting errors are generally within an acceptable range relative to the spatial and temporal
variability of the sedimentary nitrogen signal and do not compromise the overall interpretation
of large-scale TN and δ¹⁵N patterns.
We also acknowledge that our acidification control analyses primarily focused on limited
terrestrial materials and estuarine and nearshore areas influenced by riverine inputs. However,
carbonate sources and composition vary substantially across marine regions, and the effects of
terrestrial supply versus marine inputs, as well as their associated fractions and biogeochemical
processes, on nitrogen are highly variable for different acidified treatment conditions. Future
studies should extend these investigations across latitudinal and environmental gradients, from
the coastal zone to the deep-sea setting. Such efforts would not only help validate the effects of
acidification treatments on the marine nitrogen cycle but also provide a broader reference for
understanding nitrogen dynamics under future ocean acidification scenarios.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Sun et al present a comprehensive global synthesis of nitrogen isotope (δ¹⁵N) data
from modern marine sediments, including over 8,200 surface and core-top samples
and 148 dated sediment cores spanning the past century. The authors identify
spatial patterns and centennial-scale trends in δ¹⁵N, linking them to anthropogenic nitrogen
inputs, productivity changes, and sediment dynamics. The study highlights the dual
role of marine and terrestrial processes in shaping sedimentary δ¹⁵N signals, with
particular emphasis on the contrasting trends observed in coastal versus river-
dominated continental margins.
This is an important and timely contribution to our understanding of how anthropogenic
and climatic drivers have reshaped the marine nitrogen cycle over the past century.
The global scope, high-resolution temporal data, and integration of inorganic and
organic nitrogen forms provide a robust framework for interpreting δ¹⁵N variability.
However, the manuscript would benefit from streamlining and clearer separation
between the introduction, results, and discussion sections. The figures are generally
clear and informative, though their large number makes it challenging for readers to
navigate and identify the central message.
I recommend this paper for publication in Nature Communications with major revisions.
Response: Many thanks for your thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript.
We greatly appreciate the recognition of the significance of our study, including its global scope,
high-resolution temporal data, and the integration of inorganic and organic nitrogen forms,
as well as the emphasis on the dual role of marine and terrestrial processes in shaping sedimentary
δ¹⁵N signals. Regarding the suggestions for improvement: We have revised the manuscript to
improve clarity and flow. Specifically, the Introduction now focuses on setting the context and
research objectives. We have reorganized the figures by grouping related panels and moved
some less critical figures (Fig. 6) to the Supplementary Information to help readers focus on the
central messages. Further detailed responses and modifications are provided in the following
comments.
General comments:

which datasets are newly generated and which are compiled from previous studies.
This would help readers quickly grasp the scope and novelty of the work.

added a concise summary of the methods and a new table (Supplementary Table 1) that clearly
distinguishes newly generated datasets from those compiled from previous studies. The table
summarizes the study regions, dataset types, water depth, main variables (e.g., sample/core ID,
geographic coordinates, C, N, and stable isotopes), number of data points (and core numbers),
and data sources (literature data from this study), enabling readers to quickly grasp the scope
and novelty of our work. To further clarify, all datasets beyond the Yangtze River basin and
East China Sea are derived entirely from previously published studies.
Following your valuable suggestion, we have also added a Data Sources section providing
a brief overview of compiled literature and new measurements (Lines 532–551), followed by
detailed descriptions: “Data sources: Our database was compiled from more than 160 peer-
reviewed publications and complemented by newly generated datasets, providing a framework
to investigate the spatial and temporal variability of nitrogen characteristics in marine
sediments at regional to global scales. The compilation includes seafloor surface sediments
and primarily 137Cs/210Pb dated sediment cores, with parameters selected to capture both
nitrogen cycling and sedimentary context. Key variables include total, organic, and inorganic
nitrogen contents and isotopes, together with water depth, sedimentation rate, grain size, OC
content, and δ¹³C . Note that all datasets outside the Yangtze River basin and the East China
org
Sea are derived from previously published sources.
To better constrain the drivers of modern sedimentary δ¹⁵N signals in river-dominated
continental margins, we present new nitrogen measurements from six sediment cores (C0702,
C0803, DH3-1, DH3-2, DH5-1, and DH6-1) recovered from the East China Sea. These include
bulk sediment analyses, size-fractionated samples from core DH3-1, and refractory OC
fractions from cores C0803, CJK, and DH3-1. In addition, we conducted paired analyses on
terrestrial samples (sedimentary rocks and riverbed sediments) and marine samples (seabed
surface sediments, sediment cores, size-fractionated fractions, and suspended particulate
matter) to assess the effects of acidification and, for rocks only, chemical oxidation on nitrogen
signals. An overview of both literature-derived and newly generated datasets is provided in
Supplementary Table 1.”
The structure of the manuscript feels somewhat fragmented. The first part (global
compilation) appears disconnected from the second and third parts, which follow a
more logical progression, first examining centennial δ15N trends and then focusing on
a case study of the Yangtze River system. The authors may consider whether the
manuscript could be split into two complementary papers: one focused on global
patterns and drivers of δ15N, and the other on historical changes under
anthropogenic influence.
Response: We thank you for this thoughtful and constructive comment. We agree that the
manuscript consists of three distinct but interconnected components: (i) a global compilation
of marine sedimentary δ¹⁵N data, (ii) an analysis of centennial-scale δ¹⁵N and nitrogen trends,
and (iii) a detailed investigation of the Yangtze River–East China Sea system. Our rationale for
integrating these components into a single manuscript is to first establish a global baseline of
δ¹⁵N patterns, then examine how these signals have evolved over the past century, and finally
test the mechanistic insights in a representative river-dominated continental margin.
The first component (i) was designed to document the global spatial distribution of δ¹⁵N
and to evaluate its primary drivers (e.g., water depth, modern sedimentation rates, and marine
productivity). By comparing δ¹⁵N with organic and inorganic nitrogen fractions, we confirmed
that the large-scale patterns are predominantly controlled by marine processes. Building on this
framework, we then reconstructed centennial time series of δ¹⁵N and N content from sediment
cores (ii), which allowed us to investigate the imprint of anthropogenic perturbations on the
sedimentary nitrogen signals. This analysis revealed the contrasting responses of sedimentary
δ¹⁵N in river-dominated continental margins compared with other coastal systems.
To further resolve these contrasts, we examined the Yangtze River–East China Sea system
(iii), one of the world’s largest river-dominated margins and thus an ideal natural laboratory for
testing the global patterns against local processes. This regional study enabled us to identify a
previously underappreciated mechanism: the increased supply of ¹⁵N-depleted refractory OC
from terrestrial sources, rather than the exclusively marine processes such as N₂ fixation or
denitrification, as a key driver of the declining δ¹⁵N trends observed in river-influenced margins.
According to your valuable comments, we have revised the manuscript to make this three-
part structure clearer and to strengthen the logical connections between them. Specifically, we
clarified the rationale for the integrated framework in Introduction (highlighting how coastal
systems have responded to historical anthropogenic perturbations, including altered riverine N
inputs and marine N processes), streamlined transitions between these sections (e.g., from the
global spatial patterns to centennial trends: “While the global synthesis establishes a baseline
of spatial variability in sedimentary δ¹⁵N, the extent to which these signals have evolved or
remained stable in response to anthropogenic and climatic forcing remains poorly
constrained.”), and reduced redundancy to improve readability. We believe that presenting
these components together provides a more comprehensive and impactful understanding of
sedimentary nitrogen dynamics than if they were divided into two separate papers, as it directly
links global-scale patterns to regional processes under anthropogenic influence.
Given the broad readership of Nature Communications, the introduction could be
expanded to better contextualize the role of rivers in the nitrogen cycle, how these
systems have changed over the past century, and what the key drivers of those
changes are.
Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. Considering the broad readership of Nature
Communications, we have expanded the Introduction to better contextualize the role of rivers
in the nitrogen cycle, highlighting how riverine nitrogen export has changed over the past
century and the key drivers of these changes. Global riverine nitrogen export to the coastal
ocean has approximately doubled since the pre-industrial period (from the 1900s), with human
contributions increasing mainly due to agricultural intensification, land-use change, and sewage
inputs. These anthropogenic perturbations represent a major global challenge, significantly
impacting water quality and biodiversity. Elevated fluxes of ammonium, nitrate, and dissolved
organic nitrogen have raised nutrient concentrations in coastal waters, often leading to hypoxia.
Accordingly, the following text has been added to the Introduction (Lines 34–42):
“Global riverine nitrogen export to coastal systems roughly doubled from ~20 Tg N yr⁻¹
to ~42 Tg N yr⁻¹ between 1900 and 2010 (Green et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2024). The human-
induced fraction increased from ~26% to ~43% (Bouwman et al., 2005), primarily driven by
agricultural intensification, land-use change, and sewage inputs (Bouwman et al., 2005;
Schlesinger et al., 2006). This excess nitrogen has substantially altered coastal ecosystem
structure and function, driving shifts in community composition (e.g., macrophytes to fast-
growing algae, diatoms to flagellates), reducing water quality, depleting oxygen, and fostering
harmful algal blooms and eutrophication (Herbert, 1999; Howarth, 2008; Conley et al., 2009;
Voss et al., 2011; Hutchins and Capone, 2022).”

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Marine nitrogen cycle, shaped by nitrogen input and loss processes, regulates ocean productivity and leaves a distinct imprint on the ratio of stable nitrogen isotopes, δ15N. However, quantifying spatial patterns and centennial-scale variations in marine nitrogen cycling through δ15N fingerprints remains poorly constrained. Here, we present a global database of δ15N in marine sediments, comprising over 8400 seafloor samples, and create 148 time series from sediment cores spanning the past century. Our findings reveal that bulk δ15N in global marine sediments predominantly records organic matter, despite the non-negligible role of inorganic nitrogen. A widespread centennial δ15N increase, averaging 1.3‰ (interquartile range: 0.6–3.3‰) per 100 years, coinciding with total nitrogen enrichment, indicates external nitrogen inputs, productivity, and accelerated denitrification across global coastal oceans. However, in river-influenced continental margins, terrestrial sedimentary processes can obscure the 15N-enriched signal, as riverine export of 15N-depleted refractory organic matter likely lowers sedimentary δ15N.

---

## Introduction

The nitrogen (N) cycle is essential to ocean biogeochemistry1. The limited availability of nitrogen in bioavailable forms, primarily as nitrate, poses a significant nutritional constraint on phytoplankton growth, thereby influencing autotrophic carbon dioxide (CO2) fixation and marine productivity2,3. Over geological timescales, these interactions have modulated atmospheric CO2 levels and global climate patterns4–6. However, the natural marine nitrogen cycle has been profoundly altered during the Anthropocene, a period marked by escalating human impacts such as industrial agriculture, fossil fuel combustion, and land-use changes7–9. Global riverine nitrogen export to coastal systems roughly doubled from ~20 Tg N yr−1 to ~42 Tg N yr−1 between 1900 and 201010,11. The human-induced fraction increased from ~26% to ~43%12, primarily driven by agricultural intensification, land-use change, and sewage input12,13. This excess nitrogen has substantially altered coastal ecosystem structure and function, driving shifts in community composition (e.g., macrophytes to fast-growing algae, diatoms to flagellates), reducing water quality, depleting oxygen, and fostering harmful algal blooms and eutrophication3,14–17. Paradoxically, river damming and sediment retention have simultaneously reduced the flux of fluvial particulates, including nitrogen, to global coastal oceans by 49% between the 1950s and 2010s9. Although eutrophication and deoxygenation can enhance carbon preservation, long-term sedimentary carbon burial is closely tied to sediment delivery18. A decline in global fluvial particulate input reduces marine sediment accumulation9, increases oxygen exposure and organic matter remineralization19,20, and consequently diminishes sedimented carbon storage, potentially enhancing CO2 emissions to the atmosphere and generating negative climate feedbacks. These dual pressures underscore the urgent need to unravel how marine nitrogen cycling is adapting to anthropogenic perturbations and to assess the cascading effects on marine biodiversity, carbon storage, and global climate feedbacks.

Marine biogeochemical processes fractionate nitrogen isotopes (15N to 14N), generating measurable differences in the 15N/14N ratio, expressed as δ15N ([(15N/14N)sample / (15N/14N)ref –1] × 1,000‰)21. These differences arise from the production of nitrogen-bearing organic matter in the surface ocean and its subsequent burial in sediments. Nitrogen fixation produces nitrate with slightly depleted δ15N values (−4‰ to 0‰) due to minor negative isotopic fractionation relative to atmospheric N2 5,22. In contrast, denitrification and anammox processes preferentially release isotopically light 14N into the atmosphere21,23, leaving behind a 15N-enriched oceanic nitrate pool with δ15N elevated by 10–25‰5. As a result, δ15N of sinking organic matter is preserved in marine sediments, providing critical insights into past nutrient utilization, atmospheric CO2 concentration, and nitrogen source dynamics4,6,23–25. However, traditional paleoceanographic archives from deep-sea sediment cores—often characterized by low sedimentation rates—primarily resolve glacial–interglacial or millennial-scale variability, offering limited temporal resolution for studying Anthropocene-era changes confined to surface sediment layers4,6,25–28. Consequently, global reconstructions of decadal to centennial δ15N shifts in modern marine sediments remain sparse, hindering our ability to assess how anthropogenic perturbations are altering nitrogen cycling in today’s rapidly changing oceans.

Recent studies reveal that primary nitrogen isotopic signals related to surface ocean productivity are often obfuscated in bulk sedimentary δ15N of organic matter29,30. This obfuscation may arise from early diagenesis, such as organic matter remineralization during sinking and burial31,32, and contributions from both organic and inorganic nitrogen (IN) derived from terrestrial or distal marine sources, particularly in continental margins33–35. These processes modify the nitrogen signal exported to and preserved in sediments, biasing interpretations of past nitrogen utilization, budgets, and cycling dynamics. The complexity of marine nitrogen sources and cycling complicates the use of bulk δ15N as a robust tracer of modern global nitrogen biogeochemical cycles.

In this study, we conducted a global-scale analysis of seafloor sediments, expanding pioneering observations to include modern sediment records from the past century. Our database comprises over 8400 globally distributed sediment samples—including 3833 surface sediments and 189 radiometrically dated cores—collected from latitudes 69°S to 90°N and depths <10m to >7000m, encompassing coastal to abyssal zones (Supplementary Table 1). We incorporated data on inorganic and organic nitrogen to identify the sources of sedimentary total nitrogen and the drivers of spatial variability in bulk δ15N. Subsequently, we constructed 148 δ15N and 120 total nitrogen time series from dated marine sediment cores to investigate their responses to environmental perturbations. To disentangle the confounding effects of heterogeneous terrigenous inputs, sedimentation dynamics, and biological production, we prioritize the East China Sea as a representative continental shelf system (Supplementary Fig. 1). Our investigation aims to address three key questions: (i) What spatiotemporal patterns characterize sedimentary δ15N in modern oceans over the past century? (ii) How have anthropogenic forcing and climate change reshaped marine nitrogen cycling, as evidenced by sedimentary δ15N trends? (iii) What mechanisms govern sedimentary δ15N shifts across diverse marine settings? Here, we present the global assessment of centennial-scale changes in sedimentary δ15N and nitrogen content in modern marine sediments. We begin with a synoptic overview of sedimentary nitrogen species and their isotopic composition, followed by a quantitative analysis of potential environmental drivers shaping the spatial and temporal patterns of δ15N. By synthesizing this unprecedented dataset, we provide critical insights into the drivers of sedimentary δ15N variability and the role of anthropogenic perturbations in altering marine nitrogen cycling.

---

## Results

Global distributions of nitrogen isotopes in seafloor sediments
By synthesizing δ15N measurements from previously published studies of modern seafloor sediment samples, including seabed surface sediments and core tops, we generated a high-resolution global spatial pattern of δ15N (Fig. 1a). Our findings regarding the geographical characteristics of sedimentary δ15N closely align with prior simulations from ocean-biogeochemical models36 and matches observed δ15N patterns in surface nitrate and particulate organic matter26,37–39. Globally, sedimentary δ15N exhibits statistically (Kruskal–Wallis test) significant latitudinal variation at 1° bins (P<0.05) and discrete zonal differences across ocean regions (P<0.05), indicating regional heterogeneity despite minimal overall longitudinal trends (Fig. 1b). Pronounced isotopic gradients are confined to dynamic frontal zones26,40, reflecting sharp transitions between biogeochemical regimes. Latitudinal variability in δ15N is generally consistent across ocean basins, reflecting large-scale gradients in nutrient utilization associated with phytoplankton uptake25. Nevertheless, regional anomalies occur in regions influenced by strong upwelling, oxygen minimum zones, and riverine inputs29,35,41. Low-latitude marginal regions (30°N–30°S) under equatorial upwelling influence display elevated δ15N (4.4–11.3‰), with maxima in high-nutrient, suboxic systems of the subtropical Southeastern Pacific and Arabian Sea—key zones of water-column denitrification and influenced by nitrogen sources such as nitrogen from deep-water nitrate and/or horizontally advected nitrate37,41,42. In contrast, high-latitude regions such as the Antarctic/subantarctic (south of 45°S) and the western Pacific (~45°N) display 15N-depleted signatures. Although this pattern appears consistent with previous reports of intense N2 fixation in phosphorus- and iron-limited waters1,43–45, it more likely reflects the mixing of low-δ15N nitrate, terrestrial inputs, and variable nutrient utilization (e.g., limited N2 fixation in the Southern Ocean)46,47. In the Arctic (>75°N), subarctic (~55°N), and mid-latitude transition zones (30–45°S), δ15N values are elevated compared to neighboring latitudes and display greater variability. High-latitude systems exhibit distinct isotopic partitioning that primarily reflects the degree of nitrate utilization37.

These spatial patterns underscore that nitrogen loss via denitrification and anammox primarily drives modern bulk sedimentary δ15N values, yielding a global median of 5.5‰ (interquartile range, IQR: 4.3–6.8‰, N=8260; Fig. 1a)—higher than oceanic nitrate δ15N (~5.0‰)48,49. Latitudinal δ15N trends align closely with surface suspended particulate nitrogen isotope, even within Pacific-specific data constraints37, indicating sedimentary preservation of water-column nitrogen cycling signals. This linkage is reinforced by a positive δ15N–δ13Corg correlation (R=0.377, P<0.001, N=4631; Fig. 1c), suggesting that nitrogen-rich sinking particulate organic matter effectively transfers surface ocean isotopic signatures to sediments. While δ13Corg and δ15N are not always correlated, covariation can occur in marine systems where both are influenced by overlapping sources and processes. δ13Corg reflects the balance between marine and terrestrial organic matter, and δ15N records nutrient cycling in the surface ocean50. Enhanced marine productivity can simultaneously enrich δ13Corg and δ15N, whereas greater terrestrial input tends to lower both50–52. Such a moderate correlation suggests secondary variability, with additional processes—such as differences in organic matter and nitrogen sources30, diagenetic alteration31, and regional variations in nutrient utilization25—likely contribute to the scatter in the δ15N–δ13Corg relationship.

Modern sedimentary δ15N measurements reveal a globally non-normal distribution, with a median value ~20% lower than prior mean estimates (~7‰) based on limited datasets5,40. We note that over 90% of the analyzed samples originate from coastal regions (water depth <2000m)53, where median δ15N (5.8‰), δ13Corg (−22.5‰), and nitrogen content (0.13%) differ markedly from deep-sea (>2000m) samples (δ15N=7.2‰, δ13Corg =−20.0‰, TN=0.14%) (Fig. 1a, d). These disparities highlight the potential for geographical heterogeneity and terrestrial influences on sedimentary nitrogen dynamics to be overlooked when relying on global mean δ15N values.

To assess the extent to which geographical disparities and associated terrestrial processes control the global distribution of δ15N in seabed sediments, we evaluated water depths and sedimentation rates as indicators for marine environment conditions. We identified statistically significant correlations (P<0.001) between sedimentary δ15N and both water depth (positive, Fig. 1d) and modern sedimentation rates (negative, Fig. 1e), suggesting that, in addition to marine processes, terrestrial influences may contribute substantially to global δ15N variability. High sedimentation rates also occur in upwelling regions with minimal terrestrial influence, where elevated sedimentary δ15N reflects the deposition of marine organic matter sustained by upwelling54. Notably, the mobilization of IN (primarily clay-bound NH4+) from terrestrial sources has been recognized as a non-negligible contributor to marine sedimentary nitrogen burial31,33–35,55. However, interpretations of δ15N in marine sediments remain challenging, as they typically assume invariant mineral-associated nitrogen source signatures and neglect spatial heterogeneity in post-depositional alteration processes30.

To elucidate the role of IN in shaping sedimentary nitrogen signals, we quantified its content in marine sediments using both seafloor surface and core samples. While data derive predominantly from the Western Pacific, Circum-Arctic, Antarctic, and Eastern Atlantic regions, our dataset spans a bathymetric range (200–5000m). Challenging previous assumptions that IN impacts are largely restricted to coastal systems receiving illite-rich clays, such as river-dominated margins30, our analysis reveals pronounced regional variability in IN within marine sediments (0–0.11%; median ~0.03%), accounting for ~32.4% (IQR: 22.1–43.0%; N=810) of total nitrogen (Fig. 2a). Although elevated IN concentrations occur in coastal zones influenced by direct fluvial and glacial inputs (e.g., Spitsbergen continental margin, South China Sea, and Arctic fjords)34,35,56, substantial contributions in deep-sea environments (e.g., western subarctic Pacific) likely reflect aeolian dust deposition and lateral advection of terrigenous clays through ocean currents33,57.

Comparative analysis of nitrogen forms indicates that δ15N values of IN (δ15NIN) in marine sediments (median: 3.9‰, IQR: 3.2–4.8‰; non-normal distributions) are systematically 1.6‰ lower than those of δ15N of organic nitrogen (δ15NON; 5.5‰, 4.9–6.1‰) and δ15Nbulk (Fig. 2b–d). This implies that terrigenous IN input may dilute δ15Nbulk signal towards low values, especially in IN-rich continental margin sediments (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Furthermore, increasing IN contributions correlate with a negative δ15NIN shift (Fig. 2e, f), likely driven by the amplified influence of 13C-depleted refractory terrigenous organic matter in organic-poor sediment fractions30,31,57.

In continental margins influenced by terrestrial inputs, such as the East China Marginal Seas affected by rivers and high-latitude fjords, organic nitrogen can be interpreted as a binary mixture of terrestrial-derived and marine production. We propose that the delivery of 15N-depleted terrigenous organic matter drives the low δ15NON values in marine sediments, supported by a positive correlation between water depth and δ15NON (R=0.683, P<0.0001, N=134, Supplementary Fig. 2b). Although diagenetic alteration—specifically, the preferential loss of 14N during remineralization of sedimentary organic matter, enhanced in deep, oxygenated sediments—may bias this interpretation32,58, the lack of correlation between ON content and δ15NON suggests that diagenesis does not dominantly influence these isotopic signals (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Our findings contribute to mounting evidence that terrestrial influences—both inorganic and organic—must be considered alongside established processes (e.g., denitrification, N2 fixation, and internal nitrate cycling by phytoplankton)1,26 to fully interpret sedimentary δ15Nbulk and δ15NON signals in marine systems. δ15NON closely tracks δ15Nbulk (R=0.796, P<0.001, N=578; Fig. 2g), with deviations likely driven by clay-bound inorganic nitrogen30, terrigenous organic nitrogen33, and organic nitrogen mineralization32. These patterns suggest that inorganic nitrogen effects are eclipsed by marine productivity and water column denitrification. Consequently, δ15Nbulk remains a robust archive for reconstructing phytoplankton nitrate consumption in regions minimally impacted by terrigenous inputs4,23,58–60. While the global synthesis establishes a baseline of spatial variability in sedimentary δ15N, the extent to which these signals have evolved or remained stable in response to anthropogenic and climatic forcing remain poorly constrained.

Decadal to centennial changes in global marine sedimentary δ15N
Reconstructing historical nitrogen cycling using δ15N preserved in modern marine sediments provides an alternative approach to evaluate global-scale drivers of δ15N variability. Our database comprises 148 sedimentary δ15N records, spanning decadal to centennial timescales (Fig. 3). Core sites are globally distributed, predominantly along continental margins (water depth <2000m), where high sedimentation rates (mean = 0.82 cm yr⁻¹; range: 0.03–5.22 cm yr⁻¹) prevail. These records encompass margins of North and South America, East Asia, the North Indian Ocean, Australia, and the Southeast Atlantic, capturing modern climatic conditions and levels of anthropogenic influence. Elevated sedimentation rates in these coastal regions likely minimize diagenetic alteration27,59,60, enhancing the reliability of sedimentary δ15N as a tracer of nitrogen cycle dynamics.

Analysis of an extensive set of high-resolution sediment cores (AD 1900–present) reveals that no coherent global signal in sedimentary δ15N, suggesting minimal consistent decadal-to-centennial changes in marine nitrogen cycling. Of 148 sites analyzed, 97 (65%) exhibited significant temporal trends (P<0.05), with 63 sites showing increases and 34 decreases, while the remaining 51 (35%) showed no significant change (P>0.05). Notably, significant increasing trends outnumbered decreasing trends by nearly 2:1. Sedimentary δ15N increased at a rate of 1.5‰ per century (range: 1.2–2.2‰ per century) in sites with positive trends, compared to a decline of −1.2‰ per century (range: −2.3 to −0.9‰ per century) in sites with negative trends. This increase in sedimentary δ15N aligns with a doubling of riverine nitrogen export to the oceans (1900–2010)10,11, a 4.6% increase in net primary productivity in coastal oceans (1960–2010)61, and a 2.19% yr−1 rise in global coastal phytoplankton bloom frequency (2003–2020)62.

Climatic and anthropogenic factors have jointly influenced marine sedimentary δ15N trends over the past century. Sites with opposing δ15N trajectories cluster in northern tropical and temperate zones, while Southern Hemisphere data remain sparse (Fig. 3). Notably, nitrogen-rich regions with low sediment accumulation rates predominantly exhibit rising δ15N trends toward the present (Supplementary Fig. 4). High-latitude northern sites show consistent δ15N increases, contrasting with global lacustrine records that report declines in cold, nitrogen-limited regions63. This divergence suggests that climatic variables such as latitude and temperature inadequately explain marine δ15N trends, implicating additional controls.

Coastal zones under intense anthropogenic pressure—characterized by population growth, industrialization, and nutrient discharge—exhibit significant increases in sedimentary δ15N over recent decades. Hotspots of rising δ15N trends are clustered along the continental margins of Europe (North-Baltic Sea, Portuguese estuaries, Spitsbergen fjords), North America (Gulf of Mexico, Chesapeake Bay, Delaware), and South America (Brazilian coast, Comau Fjord). These regions coincide with coastal systems receiving excess nutrients from riverine inputs, wastewater discharge, groundwater infiltration, and atmospheric deposition11,64,65. Supporting for this hypothesis, our analysis of 120 global marine sediment cores reveals a century-long enrichment trend in sedimentary N burial in marine sediments (Fig. 4). Of these, 104 sites (~87%) exhibited increasing trends in N content or accumulation rates over time. Among these, 81 sites showed statistically significant trends (P<0.05), with an average rate of 1.55% per century. These spatial patterns of enhanced sedimentary N burial align closely with globally observed increases in sedimentary δ15N values during the same period. Thus, the observed 15N enrichment can be attributed to elevated inputs of high-δ15N nitrate (10–20‰) from wastewater65,66 and isotopic fractionation during phytoplankton nutrient uptake and enhanced denitrification in response to eutrophication67.

Carbon isotopic data indicate that dramatic δ15N shifts coincide with elevated primary productivity (higher δ13Corg, Supplementary Fig. 5a), reflecting increased phytoplankton biomass and likely eutrophication61,62,64. Given widespread core coverage, increased riverine nitrogen inputs10,11, enhanced coastal productivity61, and frequent phytoplankton blooms62 over the past century, this trend may partly reflect a global link between δ15N and marine productivity68,69. Additionally, the marked rise in sedimentary δ15N can be partially attributed to the preferential degradation of fresh organic matter during sedimentation or burial, despite high sedimentation rates in coastal zones. This hypothesis is supported by significant (P<0.001) correlations between δ15N and water depth (positive) and total nitrogen content (negative) [Supplementary Fig. 5b, c]. Enhanced remineralization of exported organic matter elevates microbial respiration and oxygen demand, aligning δ15N increases with coastal hypoxic zones62,64, phytoplankton biomass expansion (post-1950s)69, and deoxygenation trends70.

Centennial δ15N declines prevail in mid- to low-latitude river-influenced continental margins (e.g., Amazon River estuary, western North America, Bohai Sea, East and South China Seas), with 76% of decreasing trends (44 of 58) occurring at 20°–50°N (Supplementary Fig. 6). Although a significant positive δ13Corg–δ15N correlation exists (P<0.001), limited alteration in δ13Corg (~2.0‰) fails to account for high variability in δ15N (Supplementary Fig. 7). The absence of δ15N enriched signatures derived from marine production may be attributed to preferential degradation of labile marine organic carbon and nitrogen in dynamic margins, where preservation efficiency is <1%71. As a result, continental margins exhibiting declining sedimentary δ15N trends are typically characterized by reduced N content or no significant increases in N burial rates (Fig. 4). Sediments in these dynamic areas experience repeated cycles of sediment reworking and deposition20, reflected by thick seafloor sediment mixed layers caused by physical perturbation and bioturbation72,73. Radiocarbon and biomarker analyses indicate that buried organic carbon in these continental margin sediments is predominantly 13C-depleted, pre-aged materials74,75, sourced from terrestrial materials and aged through sediment reworking and lateral transport76. Thus, the disconnect between riverine inputs and δ15N trends cannot be ignored.

Variations in riverine sediment supply modulate the quantity and quality of terrigenous organic matter and mineral particles, potentially reshaping marine sedimentary nitrogen dynamics, with terrestrial organic and inorganic nitrogen inputs potentially overshadowing changes in marine nitrate utilization. Despite a ~49% decline in fluvial particulate transport (1950–2010)9—notably in European and Asian regions77—expected reductions in terrestrial organic matter contributions and enhanced diagenesis due to decreased sedimentation rates20 are not reflected in δ15N trends. This paradox challenges hypotheses of increasing ¹⁵N-depleted terrestrial inputs and points to unresolved controls, such as shifts in the chemical nature of terrestrially exported nitrogen.

Terrigenous sediment transport modulates δ15N dynamics in large river-dominated continental margins
To unravel drivers of the centennial-scale decline in sedimentary δ15N, we focus on the East China Sea (ECS)—a Yangtze River-influenced system and one of the world’s largest river-dominated continental shelves (Supplementary Fig. 1). Sedimentary archives from the ECS reveal a striking divergence: while δ13Corg exhibits an increasing trend, 10 of 13 cores show coherent declines in δ15N from the early 1900s to present, with an average rate of −1.09 ± 0.48‰ per century (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9a–b). Notably, cores from ECS constitute ~21% (10 of 58) of global sedimentary records with statistically significant δ15N declines (P<0.05). Additionally, the Yangtze, like many other large rivers (e.g., Mississippi, Amazon, Ganges and Yellow) has experienced considerable increases in nutrient loading alongside declining sediment fluxes over the last half-century9,68,78,79. This dual trajectory positions the ECS as a natural laboratory to disentangle the competing effects of nutrient enrichment associated production and sediment reduction on δ15N dynamics in coastal marine sediments.

In river-dominated continental margins, terrestrial organic carbon burial rates are tightly coupled to riverine lithogenic influx19. Anthropogenic reductions in particulate load diminish sedimentation rates, limiting organic carbon burial and enhancing oxygen exposure, thereby accelerating remineralization in oxic coastal sediments20,71. Paradoxically, despite increased marine productivity (elevated δ13Corg) and remineralization, sedimentary δ15N exhibits a sustained decline—a trend inconsistent with conventional nutrient cycling models. We posit that anthropogenic perturbations may alter the composition, rather than the bulk flux of terrigenous materials, modulating nitrogen isotope signatures through selective organic matter preservation.

Dam construction and land-use changes in the Yangtze River basin have reduced sediment discharge to ~20% of pre-dam levels (Supplementary Fig. 9c), triggering riverbed erosion and grain-size coarsening in both suspended and seabed sediments80. This trajectory mirrors global patterns observed in the Mississippi81, Colorado82, and Yellow River83 systems. Across the ECS, 86% of records (6 of 7) declining fine clay content (<4 μm) since 1900, with 71% (5 of 7) showing statistically significant trends (P<0.05; Supplementary Fig. 9d). These mineralogical shifts correlate strongly with δ15N depletion, indicating that terrigenous particle size distributions regulate organic nitrogen sequestration efficiency, with finer sediments enhancing preservation of 15N-enriched organic matter (primarily for marine-derived OC).

To disentangle the effects of sediment supply and hydrodynamic sorting on the marine nitrogen signal, we analyzed sedimentary δ15N against clay content and terrestrial endmember δ15N signatures (Fig. 5a, b; Supplementary Table 2). Coarse sediments predominantly host 15N-depleted woody debris and fossil-related carbon, while fine clay fractions retain 15N-enriched soil and marine OC84. Particulate δ15N remains consistent (P>0.05) from riverine inputs to seafloor deposits (Fig. 5b), indicating minimal isotopic alteration during rapid transport and burial in high-sedimentation-rate margins.

Size-fractionated analyses in core DH3-1 from the inner shelf of the East China Sea reveal divergent δ15N trajectories: the <63μm fraction shows increasing δ15N, whereas the >63μm fraction exhibits declining values, paralleling bulk sediment trends (Supplementary Fig. 10 and Table 3). Despite the dominance of fine sediments, 15N-depleted organic matter in coarse refractory materials persists and is unlikely to be offset by the 15N-enriched fine minerals that have incorporated marine carbon. We attribute this to anthropogenic mobilization of 15N-depleted refractory OC (e.g., vascular plant detritus, fossil carbon) into coastal zones via dam releases and petroleum inputs85–87, driving centennial δ15N declines.

To isolate refractory OC’s role, we applied a chemical oxidation approach to remove labile OC (Methods). This analysis allows us to reveal the signals and contribution of nitrogen associated with recalcitrant, degraded sedimentary organic matter88,89 and assess its historical changes (Supplementary Tables 4–7). This chemical oxidation eliminated ~80% of the total OC on average but only ~20% of nitrogen, doubling the N/C ratio (Fig. 5c). Near-identical intercepts for bulk and refractory C-N regressions (0.019% vs. 0.022%) exclude inorganic nitrogen as a major influence. We find that nitrogen associated with refractory organic carbon strongly correlates with bulk nitrogen across cores (P<0.05; Supplementary Fig. 11), suggesting that variance in bulk nitrogen abundance is primarily controlled by nitrogen associated with refractory OC. Compared to bulk OC, the depleted isotope signatures in refractory, with a reduction of ~2.6‰ in δ13Corg (median = −26.3‰, ranging from −28‰ to −23.5‰) and ~2.3‰ in δ15N (median = 2.1‰, ranging from −12‰ to 6.5‰), aligning with terrigenous C3 plant and petrogenic sources (Fig. 5d). Due to their chemical recalcitrance, these materials can preserve depleted δ15N signatures during transport and burial in marine sediments. Supporting this interpretation, the low C/N ratios of refractory OC likely reflect 13C-depleted terrestrial inputs, particularly petrogenic OC derived from sedimentary rocks in the Yangtze basin (e.g., shale, sandstone/siltstone, marlstone, limestone), which inherently exhibit low C/N ratios (2–6; Supplementary Table 8), consistent with previously reported bedrock data from Taiwan90.

Two mechanisms linked to the supply and sequestration of 15N-depleted refractory terrestrial OC may account for the broad declines in sedimentary δ15N observed over the past 1–2 centuries. Although terrestrial particulate load has decreased overall, anthropogenic perturbations—including land-use changes and fossil fuel combustion—appear to enhance the mobilization of refractory riverine OC87,89. This increased flux of 15N-depleted terrestrial OC into marine sediments could dilute sedimentary δ15N values30,31, a hypothesis corroborated by concurrent increases in the burial flux and contribution of 13C-depleted refractory OC in sedimentary records. Notably, the preferential degradation of labile organic matter, which typically enriches residual δ15N37, may fail to offset the 15N-depleted signature of refractory OC under these conditions. We propose that declining sedimentation rates, coupled with intensified remineralization of labile OC during particle sinking, amplify the influence of 15N-depleted organic matter on sedimentary nitrogen pools. This mechanism explains the absence of rising δ15N trends in most studied ECS sediment cores.

Globally, sedimentary δ15N records from the past century exhibit no consistent directional shift. In coastal regions, however, high-resolution sedimentary records reveal enrichment in both sedimentary δ15N and N content, likely driven by processes such as anthropogenic nitrogen inputs, enhanced productivity, water-column denitrification, and hypoxia10–12,61,62,64,69,91. Conversely, in river-dominated continental margins, human activities enhance the delivery and burial of 15N-depleted, refractory terrigenous OC, overwhelming signals of nitrate utilization and driving δ15N declines in modern sediments. This divergence between coastal and river-dominated systems has rapidly reshaped global sedimentary δ15N patterns, with nitrogen sources in river-influenced regions shifting from marine production to terrestrial dominance.

The heterogeneity in δ15N trends underscores the necessity of investigating local sedimentary processes on continental margins. Recent changes in marine nitrogen cycling cannot be attributed solely to inventory-altering (e.g., N2 fixation) or internal-cycling (e.g., denitrification) fractionation processes1,26,36. Unlike deep-sea environments, terrestrial inputs, isotopic fractionation during transport, and sediment dynamics may collectively govern δ15N evolution in modern continental margin sediments.

Additionally, our compiled global dataset includes both acidified and untreated marine sediment samples. Although acidification can introduce unintended shifts in TN and δ15N—primarily linked to carbonate characteristics, the isotopic composition of associated nitrogen, and the susceptibility of different N-containing compounds to acid treatment92–96—these effects are minor relative to the spatial and temporal variability of sedimentary nitrogen and do not compromise large-scale patterns relevant to the objectives of this work. Future work spanning latitudinal and environmental gradients, from coastal zones to the deep sea, will be essential to further constrain the effects of different acidification methods and refine interpretations of nitrogen dynamics under future ocean acidification scenarios.

Sedimentary δ15N remains a robust archive of past nitrogen cycle dynamics, and has constrained how the evolution of nitrogen burial in modern marine sediments in response to recent environmental changes. Centennial-scale trends suggest that anthropogenic perturbations and climate change may drive oceanic nitrogen cycling further from steady-state equilibria, accelerating rates of change. To refine δ15N interpretations, future work must prioritize: constraining terrigenous nitrogen sources and isotopic alterations during organic matter transport; expanding spatial coverage of centennial δ15N records, particularly in understudied deep-sea sediments; compound-specific and fossil-bound δ15N analyses29,97; and integration with isotopic models to disentangle biogeochemical drivers36,38. Addressing these gaps is critical for resolving uncertainties in the marine nitrogen budget and tracing the depositional fate of nitrogen in global marine sediments.

## Methods

Data sources
Our database was compiled from more than 160 peer-reviewed publications and complemented by newly generated datasets, providing a framework to investigate the spatial and temporal variability of nitrogen characteristics in marine sediments at regional to global scales. The compilation includes seafloor surface sediments and primarily 210Pb/137Cs dated sediment cores, with parameters selected to capture both nitrogen cycling and sedimentary context. Key variables include total, organic, and inorganic nitrogen contents and isotopes, together with water depth, sedimentation rate, grain size, OC content, and δ13Corg. Note that all datasets outside the Yangtze River basin and the East China Sea are derived from previously published sources.

To better constrain the drivers of modern sedimentary δ15N signals in river-dominated continental margins, we present nitrogen measurements from six sediment cores (C0702, C0803, DH3-1, DH3-2, DH5-1, and DH6-1) recovered from the East China Sea. These include bulk sediment analyses, size-fractionated samples from core DH3-1, and refractory OC fractions from cores C0803, CJK, and DH3-1. In addition, we conducted paired analyses on terrestrial samples (sedimentary rocks and river bed sediments) and marine samples (seabed surface sediments, sediment cores, size-fractionated fractions, and suspended particulate matter) to assess the effects of acidification and, for rocks only, chemical oxidation on nitrogen signals. An overview of both literature-derived and newly generated datasets is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Literature dataset compilation
Data on sample location, nitrogen content, bulk δ15N, δ13Corg, and chronology for seabed surface and sediment cores were extracted directly from tables or obtained via correspondence with authors. Where original data files were unavailable, values were digitized from published figures using PlotDigitizer (v. 1.3). All δ15N values are reported relative to atmospheric N2.

A global compilation of 8260 bulk δ15N measurements from modern marine sediments was assembled to map spatial trends. To evaluate the influence of inorganic nitrogen (primarily lattice-bound NH4+ in clay minerals) on marine sedimentary nitrogen pool, additional datasets were incorporated, including inorganic-to-organic nitrogen ratios (N=760) and their isotopic compositions (δ15NIN, N=512; δ15NON, N=560). The contribution and isotopic composition of ON were determined by indirect mass–balance calculations from TN and IN isotopic compositions after ON removal with KOBr–KOH solution31,33,34, and by direct δ15N measurements following organic matter isolation with HF–HCl digestion and polymer columns35,98.

Regional δ15N trends were assessed using 148 sediment cores spanning the past ~120 years, selected based on availability of water depth, modern sedimentation rates, total N content, bulk δ15N, and δ13Corg data. Evolution of N burial (content or accumulation rate) in marine sediments was reconstructed using 120 globally distributed sediment cores. Chronologies were established primarily using 210Pb models and 137Cs time markers, partly constrained by 239+240Pu, 14C, or other tracers. The choice of a age model was based on the goodness of fit, local fallout of 137Cs, recommendations from the original published studies, and the authors’ interpretation. Our reconstruction primarily applies to continental margin sediments with high sedimentation rates, and it poorly resolves low-sedimentation deep-sea sediment deposits. If the data come from sediment cores sampled during different seasons at the same location, we averaged the values of carbon and nitrogen content and isotope composition, considering these averages to be representative of temporal variability within that system.

Despite >90% of modern δ15N records originating from continental margins, spatial resolution remains insufficient to resolve small-scale features (e.g., estuaries, fjords, and continental shelves). To mitigate local heterogeneity (e.g., sediment focusing, terrestrial inputs, and energetic marine forcing), δ15N time series are expressed as relative centennial changes (Δ15N) from core-specific baselines. Data were grouped by geographic zones to assess coherent trends. Sediments with accumulation rates <0.01 cm yr−1 (e.g., deep-sea deposits) were excluded due to poor chronological resolution. Site-averaged δ15N values were assumed representative of system-wide trends, though single-core records may retain stochastic variability smoothed by regional grouping.

Sample collection and treatment
To examine terrestrial influences on sedimentary nitrogen isotope signals in river-dominated margins and their response to anthropogenic perturbations over decadal to centennial timescales, we generated high-resolution δ15N records from six marine sediment cores in the East China Sea. These cores, spanning one of the world’s largest continental shelves, were dated using 210Pb and/or 137Cs chronologies. Summaries, descriptive information, age data, models, and physical properties data were reported previously84 and references therein. Detailed site information is available in Supplementary Fig. 1.

To evaluate hydrodynamic sorting of deposited particles with distinct δ15N signatures, we performed grain-size fractionation on core DH3-1. Sediments samples were wet-sieved using stainless steel mesh (63 μm) and ultrapure water to isolate coarse (>63 μm) and fine (<63 μm) fractions. Elemental concentrations (C, N) and isotopic compositions (δ15N, δ13C) were measured for both fractions. To quantify the contribution of refractory organic matter to bulk δ15N, we applied a chemical oxidation protocol to remove labile organic carbon in four sediment cores (C0702, C0803, CJK, and DH3-1). Residual materials were analyzed for geochemical composition (OC, TN, δ15N, and δ13Corg).

To constrain the end-member of nitrogen associated with refractory OC and to evaluate the effects of acidification and chemical oxidation, we collected twenty-four sedimentary rock samples from the northeastern lower Yangtze region (Supplementary Fig. 1), part of the South China Block, which exposes strata from the Upper Precambrian to the Middle Triassic99. The sampled sedimentary rocks include marlstone, siliceous shale, shale, carbonaceous shale, sandstone, lignite, siltstone, fine sandstone, and limestone, broadly representing the main types of outcropped sedimentary rocks in the region. Detailed information on the sampling sites and sedimentary rock compositions is provided in Supplementary Table 8.

Elemental and isotopic analyses
Freeze-dried sediment samples were homogenized in an agate mortar, and inorganic carbon was removed via acid treatment following established protocols84. Briefly, decarbonation was performed using 4M HCl, followed by rinsing with deionized water and drying. Acidified aliquots were analyzed for organic carbon (OC) and total nitrogen (TN) content, as well as δ13Corg and δ15N values, using an elemental analyzer (Elementar Analysensysteme GmbH, Germany) coupled to an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (IsoPrime 100). Isotopic ratios are reported in δ notation (‰) relative to the Vienna PeeDee Belemnite (V-PDB) standard for δ13Corg and atmospheric N2 for δ15N. Calibration and quality control utilized certified standards (L-histidine, D-glutamic acid, glycine, acetanilide) and the USGS 40 reference material. Analytical precision (1σ), determined from replicate analyses of USGS 40 (N=12) and samples, was ±0.02% (OC), ±0.006% (TN), ±0.2‰ (δ15N), and ±0.3‰ (δ13Corg).

To directly evaluate the potential influence of acid pretreatment on nitrogen measurements, we analyzed 160 paired samples with and without 4M HCl treatment, spanning terrestrial (Yangtze River basin) and marine (East China Sea) environments (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 12). These included marine seabed surface sediments (N=40), five sediment cores (N=67), suspended particulate matter (N=12), grain size-fractionated (>63 μm and <63 μm) sediments (N=13), river bed materials (N=4), and sedimentary rocks (N=24), representing a wider range of TN contents and δ¹⁵N values (Supplementary Tables 8–9).

Across this diverse dataset, differences in ΔTN (TNacidfied – TNuntreated; mean = 0.01% and median = 0.007%) and Δδ15N (δ15Nacidfied – δ15Nuntreated; mean = –0.183‰, median = –0.266‰) between bulk and acidified marine samples remain well within analytical precision (0.01% for TN and 0.3‰ for δ¹⁵N) [Supplementary Fig. 12a–d] Importantly, acidification did not alter overall trends in either terrestrial or marine samples, as evidenced by highly significant (P<0.0001) and robust (R>0.91) correlations between pre- and post-treatment values (Supplementary Fig. 12e–h). Nevertheless, acid treatment can introduce unintended alterations in both ΔTN and Δδ15N values: most marine (~79%, N=104) and terrestrial (~82%, N=23) samples showed positive shifts in TN content after treatment, whereas δ15N tended to decrease in a substantial proportion of marine samples (~64%, N=84) compared with terrestrial samples (~39%, N=11) [Supplementary Fig. 13]. We attribute these patterns to a combination of factors, including the potential chemical transformation or loss of nitrogen (e.g., carbonate-associated), which may cause fractionation (posited but unknown)92–96, and the enrichment of nitrogen resulting from the removal of carbonate minerals.

Our results align with previous studies showing that acidified treatments generally yield TN and δ15N values indistinguishable from—or within the analytical precision of—untreated marine sediments, as differences between bulk and decarbonated samples typically fall within precision limits27,93,95,96. Nonetheless, we note that stronger acid treatments, particularly for N-poor samples, may induce larger deviations under certain conditions96. Applying identical procedures to sediment samples from the same core helps minimize analytical artifacts and ensure that relative trends in TN and δ15N remain robust27. Finally, whether the acid effect is considered significant depends on the specific research question93, as the shifts in both δ15N and TN induced by acid treatment are often minor relative to the large-scale patterns and variability of nitrogen signals in global marine sediments (Figs. 1, 3, and 4).

Refractory organic carbon analysis
To characterize nitrogen associated with refractory organic matter in marine sediments, we isolated chemical oxidation-resistant OC using sodium persulfate (Na2S2O8), a method simulating microbially mediated oxidative degradation88. Freeze-dried bulk samples (~0.5 g) were dispersed in 250 mL distilled water, reacted with 20 g Na2S2O8 (MACKLIN) and 22 g NaHCO3 for 48 h at 80°C, and rinsed to collect residual refractory OC. OC, TN, δ13Corg, and δ15N were measured in the residual fraction to identify terrestrial refractory OC composition and contributions. Analytical precision (1σ) for repeated measurements of oxidized residues was ±0.02% (OC), ±0.008% (TN), ±0.43‰ (δ13Corg), and ±0.24‰ (δ15N).

To evaluate potential analytical artifacts, eleven replicate blank analyses were conducted using the same protocols as for sediment samples. OC and TN contents in the aqueous phase were measured with an elemental analyzer (TOC-L, Shimadzu, Japan). The mean blank values (±1σ) were 0.408 ± 0.04 ppm for OC and 0.004 ± 0.003 ppm for TN, the latter being close to the analytical uncertainty (~0.004 ppm). These correspond to 0.023 ± 0.01% and 0.001 ± 0.0004% of typical contents in refractory marine sediments (N=75; Fig. 5c, d), respectively, confirming that blank contributions are negligible and do not affect δ13C or δ15N measurements.

The chemical oxidation approach was designed to remove labile, 13C- and 15N-enriched OC in marine sediments while preserving most refractory terrestrial carbon that is typically 13C- and 15N-depleted. To test this, paired oxidation experiments were conducted on sedimentary rock samples from the Yangtze River basin (N=24), dominated by graphitic refractory OC largely resistant to oxidation100. Chemically oxidized and unoxidized samples yielded comparable mean values for OC (1.2% vs. 1.5%), TN (0.121% vs. 0.129%), δ13Corg (–27.1‰ vs. –27.0‰), and δ15N (2.5‰ vs. 2.3‰) [Supplementary Fig. 14]. Although minor labile fractions may be removed, no significant differences were observed (P>0.05, Wilcoxon test), and isotopic values consistently fell within the terrestrial end-member range50–52.

Together, these results confirm that the oxidation treatment effectively distinguishes refractory from labile pools while minimizing isotopic artifacts. The isotopic shifts observed in marine sediments therefore reflect genuine compositional differences in organic matter rather than analytical bias. Paired datasets for bulk (unoxidized) and refractory (oxidized) rock samples are provided in Supplementary Table 10.

Statistical analysis and plotting
Data distributions were assessed for normality using the D’Agostino-Pearson test (GraphPad Prism v9.5.1) to determine the most reliable measure of central tendency. For normally distributed data, we report the mean with the 95% confidence intervals (CI). For non-normally distributed data, we instead report the median with the interquartile range (IQR, 25–75%) as a more appropriate descriptor of central tendency101,102. Group comparisons employed Student’s t-tests (two groups) or analysis of variance (ANOVA; >2 groups), with statistical significance thresholded at P<0.05. The Wilcoxon test, a nonparametric method, was used to compare two paired groups, while the Kruskal–Wallis test, also nonparametric, was applied to assess differences among three or more independent groups.

For temporal δ15N trends, linear regressions between sediment age and δ15N values were performed on each core spanning the past 100–120 years. To standardize records, δ15N time series were expressed as deviations from core-specific baselines (Δ15N). Regional patterns were inferred by grouping 148 globally distributed cores into geographic sets, accounting for bathymetric variability. Bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals of linear fits for δ15N were generated from 10,000 iterations using Acycle103. The global distribution map of data points was created and downloaded using the open-access online platform ChiPlot (https://www.chiplot.online/)104,105.
